pain_cycle.title: Breaking the Pain Cycle
points: Pain can make you move less.
Moving less weakens muscles, so moving gets harder.
Easing pain and rebuilding strength can break the cycle.
explain: Pain leads to less activity, which causes muscle weakness and loss of conditioning, making stairs, chairs and distance harder and reducing activity further.
The cycle does not mean every increase in pain reflects worsening structural damage; pain, movement and physical capacity influence one another.
The aim is not to eliminate all discomfort first, but to reduce symptoms enough to allow safe, sustainable activity and better function.
options: Education, exercise and physical therapy
Weight management, medications and assistive devices
GAE or orthopedic care when indicated
ask: What has your knee pain stopped you from doing?
How far can you walk, and how are stairs and chairs?
Has the pain affected your sleep or mood?
refer: Rapid loss of function or inability to bear weight.
Persistent low mood or hopelessness: discuss support and treatment.
Hot, swollen joint with fever: urgent evaluation for infection.
pain_cycle.alt: Circular diagram in which pain with walking or stairs leads to less activity, weaker muscles, harder movement and even less activity, with “Break the cycle: treat pain + rebuild strength” in the center.

types.title: Arthritis Is Not One Disease
points: More than 100 conditions can affect the joints.
Each type has different causes and treatments.
An accurate diagnosis is always the first step.
explain: Osteoarthritis is the most common form and is a whole-joint condition affecting cartilage, bone, synovium and surrounding tissues.

Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic and related) is immune-driven and needs rheumatology care; post-traumatic arthritis follows fractures, ligament tears or other injuries that change joint shape or loading.
Crystal arthritis such as gout causes sudden, intensely painful flares, often in the big toe; non-arthritic causes such as tendon, meniscal, bursal or nerve problems should also be considered.
options: OA: foundation care, then injections, GAE or surgery as needed
Inflammatory arthritis: rheumatology-directed treatment
Gout: crystal-specific treatment; injury: address mechanics
ask: Have you had a past injury, fracture or surgery on this joint?
Do other joints swell, or does morning stiffness last long?
Have you had sudden attacks of severe pain and swelling?
refer: Symmetric small-joint swelling or prolonged morning stiffness: rheumatology.
Sudden hot, red, swollen joint: evaluate for gout or infection.
Fever with a painful joint: urgent evaluation for septic arthritis.
types.alt: Four cards describing types of arthritis: osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis, post-traumatic arthritis and crystal arthritis, each with a simple joint icon.

pain_patterns.title: Understanding Pain Patterns
points: Pain with use that eases with rest is common in OA.
Stiffness, swelling or warmth may point to inflammation.
Tell us about night pain and what activities trigger it.
explain: Mechanical pain relates to movement or loading, rising with walking, stairs or standing and easing with rest; OA commonly has a mechanical component.
Prolonged morning stiffness, persistent swelling, warmth and multiple-joint involvement may suggest inflammatory or infective arthritis.
Night pain can occur with more advanced OA, but unexplained or severe night pain, systemic symptoms or a rapidly changing pattern warrant further evaluation.
options: Mechanical OA pain: foundation care and load management
Inflammatory features: lab tests and rheumatology input
Imaging matched to the question: X-ray first, MRI if needed
ask: Does the pain get worse with activity and better with rest?
How long does stiffness last when you first get up?
Does pain wake you at night, and which activities trigger it?
refer: Severe or unexplained night pain, or pain with fever or weight loss.
Rapidly changing pain pattern: investigate other causes.
Multiple swollen, warm joints: evaluate for inflammatory arthritis.
pain_patterns.alt: Four panels describing mechanical pain, inflammatory pain, rest and night pain, and activity-related symptoms, each with an icon such as a person climbing stairs or lying in bed.

foundation.title: Building the Foundation
points: Learning about OA and staying active is the base.
Exercise and physical therapy build strength and mobility.
Other treatments build on this base; they don’t replace it.
explain: Major guidelines identify education, exercise and weight management when relevant as core components of OA care.
Exercise should be individualized and progressed over time, including quadriceps, hamstring and hip strengthening, mobility, aerobic and balance training.
Bracing, canes, heat or cold, topical or oral NSAIDs, duloxetine and short-term injections complement this foundation; GAE is also meant to work alongside it, not replace it.
options: Education, goal-setting and pacing activity
Progressive exercise and physical therapy
Weight management, devices and medications as needed
ask: What exercise or therapy have you done, and for how long?
Did your program include strengthening, and was it progressed?
What has made it hard to keep up with your exercises?
refer: Persistent pain despite an adequate foundation trial: discuss next-step options.
Oral NSAID use with heart, stomach or kidney risks: review safety.
Sharp pain, or swelling lasting more than a day or two after exercise: reassess the program.
foundation.alt: Five-level pyramid with education and self-management at the base, then exercise and physical therapy, weight management, supportive devices, and medications and symptom tools at the top.

vessels.title: Blood Vessels and Knee Pain
points: An inflamed joint lining can grow new, abnormal vessels.
These vessels may help keep inflammation and pain going.
GAE is designed to reduce these abnormal vessels.
explain: In OA, inflamed synovium releases cytokines and growth factors such as VEGF that promote angiogenesis, and the new vessels may carry in more inflammatory cells.
Sensory nerves may grow in alongside new vessels, and inflammatory mediators can sensitize nerve endings, which may contribute to persistent pain.
This is one of several contributors to multifactorial OA pain; GAE aims to interrupt the loop at the vessel step, and these mechanisms remain under investigation.
options: Foundation care for mechanical and muscle contributors
Injections for short-term symptom control
GAE evaluation for persistent pain in selected patients
ask: Does your knee swell or feel warm at times?
Has the pain kept going despite exercise and medicines?
What treatments have you tried, and how did they work?
refer: Warm, swollen knee with fever: rule out infection or crystals.
Suspected inflammatory arthritis: rheumatology evaluation.
Pain mainly from the hip, spine or nerves: GAE unlikely to help.
vessels.alt: Circular diagram in which synovial inflammation leads to new blood vessels, inflammatory cells, nerve ingrowth and sensitized pain, with “GAE target: reduce abnormal vessels” in the center.

gae_inside.title: Treating From Inside the Vessels
points: A small needle puncture, usually in the groin artery.
A thin tube is guided to the knee using live X-ray.
Tiny particles reduce flow to abnormal knee vessels.
explain: Access is through a small arterial puncture, commonly femoral on either side, with radial or pedal access sometimes considered, so no incision is made at the knee.
A catheter is navigated under fluoroscopy, then a microcatheter is advanced into selected genicular branches while contrast angiography maps the anatomy.
Embolic particles are delivered slowly to reduce flow in abnormal vessels while preserving the parent artery, usually under local anesthetic with or without sedation.
options: Local anesthetic, with or without sedation
Usually outpatient with same-day discharge
Commonly about one to two hours
ask: Do you have circulation problems or leg artery disease?
Have you reacted to X-ray dye, or do you have kidney disease?
Do you take blood thinners or have bleeding problems?
refer: Significant peripheral arterial disease: vascular assessment first.
Severe kidney impairment or contrast allergy: individualized risk planning.
Bleeding disorder or anticoagulation: a safe periprocedural plan is needed.
gae_inside.alt: Leg diagram showing a catheter entering at the groin and traveling down the artery to the knee, a close-up of small vessels around the knee joint, and four numbered steps: access, navigate, select, treat.

arteries.title: The Genicular Arteries
points: A ring of small arteries surrounds the knee.
The branches differ from person to person.
Careful mapping helps protect healthy tissue.
explain: Knee blood supply includes branches associated with the popliteal artery and the descending genicular artery, including the superior and inferior medial and lateral genicular arteries.
These vessels connect through anastomoses and their branching varies, so one branch may supply more than one region, including skin.
During GAE, angiography maps this network so the specialist can treat selected abnormal branches while preserving the knee’s main blood supply.
options: Angiographic mapping before any treatment
Selective microcatheter placement
Protective steps such as cold packs on the skin
ask: Where exactly is your knee pain: inner, outer or front?
Have you had knee surgery or a knee replacement?
Do your legs cramp with walking and ease with rest?
refer: Calf, thigh or buttock pain with walking: evaluate for peripheral artery disease.
Weak or absent pulses, or a cold or discolored foot: vascular evaluation.
Non-healing leg or foot wounds: vascular evaluation.
arteries.alt: Front-view illustration of a knee joint with labeled genicular arteries: descending, superior medial and lateral, inferior medial and lateral, and the popliteal artery behind the knee.

how_gae.title: How GAE Is Designed to Work
points: An inflamed lining with extra vessels can drive pain.
X-ray dye shows these areas as a cloudy “blush.”
Tiny particles slow that flow so the joint may calm down.
explain: GAE targets synovitis with abnormal new vessels, which are thought to help sustain inflammation and interact with pain-sensitive nerves.
Angiography identifies abnormal staining, and a microcatheter delivers embolic particles to selected branches while keeping the main arteries open.
If abnormal vascularity contributes to symptoms, inflammation and pain may settle; GAE does not regrow cartilage, reverse structural OA or guarantee relief.
options: Foundation care continues before and after GAE
Injections as another option for persistent pain
Orthopedic opinion for advanced structural disease
ask: What would you do if your knee hurt less?
What have you heard about GAE, and what do you expect?
How should we measure whether a treatment has helped?
refer: Major deformity or end-stage structural OA: orthopedic evaluation.
Meniscal or ligament injury needing surgery: orthopedic referral.
Active infection or septic arthritis: treat first and defer GAE.
how_gae.alt: Four knee illustrations in sequence: an inflamed lining with abnormal vessels, angiography finding the blush, embolization with a catheter and tiny particles, and a calmer joint with less abnormal flow.

angiogram.title: What the Angiogram Shows
points: Dye makes the knee arteries visible on X-ray.
Abnormal vessels show up as a cloudy “blush.”
After treatment the blush fades; main artery stays open.
explain: Contrast angiography can show abnormal vascular staining, often called a blush, that may correspond to inflamed tissue and the patient’s painful region.
The blush is interpreted alongside pain location, anatomy and clinical findings; not every visible vessel is a treatment target.
A typical endpoint is reduced abnormal staining with flow preserved in the parent artery; the figure is a simplified illustration, not a patient image.
options: Mark the most painful spot before the procedure
Selective angiography of each candidate branch
Completion imaging to check the endpoint
ask: Can you point to the spot where it hurts most?
Have you ever reacted to X-ray dye?
Do you have kidney problems or diabetes?
refer: Prior contrast reaction: individualized plan before angiography.
Reduced kidney function: check labs and minimize contrast.
Blush that does not match the painful area: reassess the pain source.
angiogram.alt: Side-by-side simplified X-ray drawings: before, a cloudy abnormal blush of small vessels beside a branch artery; after, the blush is reduced and the main artery is still open.

side_effects.title: Side Effects at a Glance
points: Common: knee ache, bruising, tiredness for a day or two.
Less likely: skin color change, small sore, foot tingling.
Rare: dye reaction, artery injury, infection or clot.
explain: Most reported side effects are minor and short-lived; a temporary pain flare and access-site bruising or tenderness are common and usually settle within days to about two weeks.
Less likely effects include patchy skin discoloration over the knee, a small skin sore that usually heals on its own, foot tingling or numbness, and access-site hematoma, usually temporary.
Rare risks include contrast reaction, contrast-related kidney strain, artery injury, infection, blood clot and nontarget embolization injuring skin, muscle or nerve.
options: Screening for PAD, kidney function, allergy and bleeding risk
Careful mapping and slow, controlled particle delivery
Clear aftercare instructions and scheduled follow-up
ask: Do you have kidney disease, diabetes or a dye allergy?
Do you take blood thinners or have bleeding problems?
Who can drive you home and check on you that day?
refer: Groin swelling, bleeding or pain that is getting worse.
Skin breakdown, a sore, or spreading color change over the knee.
Fever, calf swelling, or a cold, numb or weak foot.
side_effects.alt: Three columns of GAE side effects: common and usually mild, less likely and occasional, and rare, each listing example effects.

decision.title: A Step-by-Step Decision Path
points: Start with your goals and an accurate diagnosis.
Build the foundation, then check if it is enough.
If not, talk through next steps that fit you.
explain: Persistent knee pain starts with defining goals and confirming the diagnosis by history, exam and X-ray, with MRI when needed; other sources are treated directly.
For knee OA, education, exercise, PT, weight management and medications come first, with reassessment after an adequate trial; if relief is enough, continue and monitor.

If not, options include injections, GAE, nerve ablation and an orthopedic opinion; mild-to-moderate, pain-driven OA may suit injections or GAE, while advanced OA with deformity warrants orthopedic evaluation.
options: Injections or GAE for mild–moderate, pain-driven OA
Nerve ablation in selected patients
Orthopedic evaluation for advanced OA or deformity
ask: What would you do if your knee hurt less?
What have you tried, for how long, and how did it work?
How will we measure success: pain, distance or an activity?
refer: Hip, spine, tendon or nerve source: treat the true source.
Inflammatory arthritis features: rheumatology referral.
Advanced OA with deformity: orthopedic surgical evaluation.
decision.alt: Flowchart from persistent knee pain to accurate diagnosis, branching to treating another source or building the OA foundation, then reassessing relief and discussing next-step options such as injections, GAE or orthopedic evaluation.

sample_week.title: A Joint-Friendly Week
points: Mix walking, swimming or biking with strength work.
Strengthen your muscles at least two days a week.
Start where you are and build up gradually.
explain: U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly plus muscle strengthening on two or more days, as able.
Low-impact choices such as level walking, cycling, swimming, water aerobics, tai chi and elliptical are generally well tolerated, and even 10 minutes at a time counts.
The week shown is an example only; a physical therapist should tailor and progress the plan, and during a flare patients should adjust activity rather than stop.
options: Physical therapy to build a tailored plan
Sit-to-stand, bridges, leg raises and step-ups
Flare plan: adjust, pace, then return gradually
ask: What activities do you enjoy or want to get back to?
How many minutes can you walk comfortably today?
What gets in the way of staying active?
refer: Hot, red, very swollen joint, fever, or inability to bear weight.
Leg pain with walking that eases with rest: check for peripheral artery disease.
A flare that does not settle within a week or two.
sample_week.alt: Seven-day schedule with walking, strength, swimming or biking, rest or stretching and tai chi sessions of 10 to 30 minutes, above weekly targets of 150 minutes of aerobic activity, 2 or more strength days and some movement every day.
